analysis.title: "At The Cusp": The Next Repo Crisis Is Already On The 2027 Calendar, And Goldman Just Published The Date
key_insights: Goldman rates strategist Isabella Rosenberg argues the benign 2026 funding backdrop should carry into 2027 with a slightly tighter baseline and a clearer case for repo volatility, because bank reserves sit 'at the cusp of the steeper part of the demand curve'.

Repo rates have traded below IORB since May. SOFR is about 2bps below IORB and tri-party repo (TGCR) about 4bps below. Goldman's model, which fits SOFR to system liquidity, bill supply, dealer repo book size and seasonals, says funding has been cheaper than fundamentals imply for much of 2H26.

Goldman attributes the calm to rangebound reserves, lower funding demand, more bank use of the Fed's standing repo operations, and regulatory changes (eSLR amendment, sponsored repo) that ease dealer intermediation. Neither more balance sheet nor less demand for it is guaranteed to persist.

Fed Reserve Management Purchases (RMPs) started at $40BN a month in December 2025, fell to $25BN in April and $10BN in May, and stopped in August. Goldman expects a restart this month at about $10BN, through at least 1Q27, then about $25BN a month from 2Q27, which it estimates keeps reserves stable as a share of bank assets. A faster pace into year-end as a precaution would not surprise Rosenberg.

Goldman expects total Fed bill purchases (RMPs plus MBS runoff reinvested into bills) to roughly double from the low-$40BN area per month from April. The $10BN x 3 months plus $25BN x 9 months works out to about $255BN of fresh reserves in 2027 before MBS reinvestment.

Goldman thinks the Fed would look through any debt-ceiling-driven liquidity surplus and would not restart QT. A later TGA rebuild could reverse the liquidity boost and raise upside risks to funding costs. The balance sheet only grows from here.

Longer run, Goldman assumes the Fed keeps buying bills until the bill share of its Treasury portfolio reaches a market-neutral level, probably in 2028, and only then spreads purchases across the curve, unless it adopts an asset-liability approach tilted toward bills and short coupons.

Goldman's steady-state assumption is reserves around 11% of bank assets, roughly the current level, but risks are skewed to the downside (the Fed may conclude the system can function with less). Warsh's balance sheet task force reports early in 1Q27. Goldman expects it to reinforce the ample reserves framework while possibly redefining 'ample'.

Dallas Fed's Logan favors an approach that reduces banks' need for reserves and shifts the demand curve inward. Goldman's options: count pre-pledged discount-window collateral and FHLB capacity toward LCR and internal liquidity stress tests, reduce stigma of Fed facilities, and let Treasury lend part of its cash in repo when rates exceed IORB.

Goldman's scatter of TGCR-IORB against reserves plus RRP as a share of bank assets shows that in the 11%-12% zone repo traded as much as 13bps above IORB in the past, but mostly 2-9bps below since April. Goldman reads this as lower reserve demand and more room for reserves to decline. The author reads it as the system being one bad week from either cluster.

The mid-2027 mandatory repo clearing deadline cuts both ways for SOFR: it should help dealer balance sheets and compress the tri-party/bilateral gap, but bringing more bilateral trades into SOFR would bias it higher. Migration to cleared repo reversed in 2026, which Goldman attributes to greater use of repo with embedded optionality, which is exempt.

Treasury supply: Goldman sees total net supply rising slightly from $2.1 trillion to $2.2 trillion in 2027, with net bill supply up about $200BN to $1.1 trillion. The portion non-Fed buyers must absorb rises to about $600BN from $480BN this year.

Goldman now expects larger coupon auction sizes from August 2027, limited to the 2Y-10Y sector, with the long end unchanged and risk skewed to modest cuts. That is three months later than the May start for 2Y-7Y that the same team had expected before last week's refunding, when Treasury dropped 'at least' from its guidance. Net coupon supply still shrinks next year. Bigger auctions push repo rates up to the extent the marginal buyer is levered.

Money market fund demand is the weak link. Bills have cheapened to OIS. Money funds took in about $800BN by year-end in both 2024 and 2025, but 2026 inflows went flat in July at about a quarter-trillion. Goldman cites strong risk-asset returns, higher long-end yields and equity vol pushing cash into long-term bond funds, and funds shortening WAMs ahead of the Fed.

For 2027 Goldman expects slightly better money fund demand and longer WAMs as risk assets cool and inflation eases, but no repeat of 2024-25 inflows. Treasury leans on a buyer base that has stopped growing while the Fed's bill bid falls from $40BN to $10BN a month. The author expects the bills-OIS cheapening to continue and notes AI debt issuance (hyperscaler term loans, data center ABS) competes for the same cash.

Goldman's funding path has the $41.1 trillion debt ceiling binding in 1Q27, most likely in February. Treasury then runs down the TGA and pays down bills, adding reserves. Over the last three episodes the TGA fell about $400BN between binding and the deal. Goldman estimates a decline of that size with matching bill paydowns is worth about 4bps of downward pressure on SOFR (about 1bp per $100BN). Treasury held nearly $1 trillion in cash as recently as August, so a larger drawdown is possible. Spring and summer 2027 could see unusually easy funding.

With Democrats taking both chambers in January and Wall Street X-date estimates clustered in 4Q27, a quick deal is not expected. After the ceiling is lifted, Treasury rebuilds cash by flooding bills, draining reserves and pushing repo up. Goldman says greater standing repo facility use and a better sense of adequate reserves should soften this versus 2025 but not remove it.

Rosenberg: the starting point of reserves determines funding volatility. In 2021 and 2023 (liquidity above 20% of bank assets) debt-limit TGA swings went unnoticed. In 2019 and 2025 (lower reserves) the post-debt-limit rebuild caused stress. Reserves plus RRP are now a little above 11% of bank assets, versus about 14% where the 2025 episode began and only a few points above the 2019 trough, so volatility could be two-way: easy funding during TGA drawdown, tight on the refill.

Goldman's house view is a final Fed hike in December (it dropped its no-hike call in September), then a hold, then three cuts from 2H27 through early 2028 taking the funds rate to 3.25%-3.5%. The author notes the funding-tightening events (TGA rebuild, bill deluge, bigger coupons from August, clearing mandate aftermath, stalled money funds) fall in the same window Goldman has the Fed starting to ease.

The author argues history is two for two: in 2019 (limit suspended early August, repo hit 10% on September 17, Fed buying $60BN of bills a month by mid-October) and 2025 (limit raised in July, record $50BN standing repo facility draw by October 31, QT ended, three cuts by year-end, $40BN monthly bill purchases by December) the Fed cut and expanded its balance sheet within months of the TGA refill. The author concludes Goldman's easing call and its late-year funding risk are probably the same event.

The author expects that a Fed still fighting 0.3% core CPI prints will not cut because repo misbehaves, so the first leg of easing will likely show up in the size of bill purchases. Goldman's $25BN a month for 2027 is described as a floor.

Macro backdrop on Nov 11, 2026: Fed Governor Waller floated a 50bps hike before October CPI printed hotter than expected, a December hike is fully priced, and the 2Y jumped to 4.61%, while the Fed is expected to restart T-bill purchases this month.

vol_and_positioning: Repo funding spreads have traded below IORB since May 2026. Goldman sees two-way funding volatility risk in 2027: easier while the TGA drains in spring and summer, tighter on the post-ceiling refill.
Banks have grown more comfortable using the Fed's standing repo operations. Record $50BN standing repo facility use on October 31, 2025 is cited as the precedent for stress.
Money fund inflows stalled at about a quarter-trillion in 2026 versus roughly $800BN in each of 2024 and 2025, and funds have shortened WAMs, which pushes bills cheaper to OIS.
The marginal repo borrower is still a levered hedge fund and the marginal lender a money market fund. Bigger coupon auctions raise repo rates to the extent the marginal buyer is levered.
geopolitical: The note refers to the Iran war as one of the dominant market concerns in 2026.
Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress in January 2027, which makes a quick debt ceiling deal unlikely.
cross_bank_references: Barclays in September expected $10BN of RMPs in October and $20BN in November (the October part did not happen).
Citi in September expected the Fed to stay on pause for the rest of the year because reserves were back in mildly abundant territory.
Morgan Stanley's Seth Carpenter: shrinking the balance sheet 'doesn't have to be symmetric... at all'.
BMO's Vail Hartman: financial markets could face a protracted debt ceiling standoff in 2027.
UBS observed on election night that Democrats are taking both chambers (per the text).
Same Goldman team had expected a May start for 2Y-7Y coupon size increases ahead of last week's refunding.

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman: the benign 2026 funding backdrop should carry into 2027. Fed RMPs and possible balance sheet changes that reduce reserve demand keep policy a stabilizing force, and greater standing repo facility use should soften a post-debt-ceiling TGA rebuild versus 2025. The market 'reasonably discounts this slightly tighter baseline'.
tension_points.bear_case: The author: with reserves a little above 11% of bank assets, the post-ceiling TGA rebuild of about $400BN drains in weeks what $25BN a month of RMPs adds in 16 months. Bill supply is rising while money fund inflows have stalled. The 2019 and 2025 refills both forced the Fed to cut and expand its balance sheet within months.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Goldman's benign baseline is invalidated by a debt-ceiling resolution followed by a TGA rebuild with reserves near 11% of bank assets, as in 2019 and 2025. Repo rates jumping above IORB would show it.

theme_stances.key_argument: Reserves at the cusp of the steeper part of the demand curve make a post-debt-ceiling TGA rebuild a risk for repo spikes, as in 2019 and 2025.
theme_stances.evidence: at the cusp of the steeper part of the demand curve

theme_stances.key_argument: The Fed stays a meaningful, price-insensitive bill buyer all of 2027 and is unlikely to restart QT, so the balance sheet only grows.
